solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Bent officer is arresting Unionist

parts.note: GEN is short for general, a senior army officer

indicators.note: to arrest is to seize and hold, so one piece takes another into custody inside it

parts.note: taken as written
U is the abbreviation for Unionist

explanation.surface: A corrupt policeman takes a Unionist politician into custody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bent' reads as crooked, describing the officer, but it is the definition in its sense of natural talent.
explanation.definitionFit: A bent for something is a natural aptitude or flair, which is one sense of genius as an exceptional gift.

clue.text: Deity wound up

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a sore is a wound or tender spot

explanation.surface: A god has been wound up like a clockwork toy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wound up' looks like one phrase meaning tightened or annoyed; split it, and 'wound' is a noun with 'up' telling you to turn it over.
explanation.definitionFit: Eros is the Greek god of love, so he is a deity.

clue.text: Step in time with Eve 'n' Erin's dancing

indicators.note: dancers move about and change places, so the letters are shuffled into a new order

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time
the letters of the two names and the n, taken as written

explanation.surface: A dancer is told to step in time with two women, Eve and Erin, as they dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Step in time' reads as a dance instruction; the definition is only 'Step in', and 'time' is part of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To intervene is to come between parties or get involved, which is what stepping in means.

clue.text: Beg to live away — adopting Portugal as address

indicators.note: to adopt is to take in as one's own, so the letter is taken inside what remains
sent away means taken out, so the word for live is removed from the longer word

parts.note: to beseech is to beg earnestly
to be is to exist or live; these letters are removed
P is the international vehicle code for Portugal

explanation.surface: Someone pleads to live abroad, giving Portugal as their home address.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Away' means the shorter word comes off the front of the longer one before the country's letter goes in. 'Address' looks like a postal location but means a formal talk.
explanation.definitionFit: An address is a formal talk delivered to an audience, the same thing as a speech.

clue.text: Friend's confronting baddies regularly — and paling

parts.note: friend is: PAL IS

indicators.note: at regular intervals means every other letter is kept, here the second, fourth and sixth

parts.note: the even letters of the word

explanation.surface: A friend is standing up to the villains and turning pale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Confronting' only places one piece in front of the other. 'Paling' looks like turning pale, but it is the noun for a fence of stakes.
explanation.definitionFit: A palisade is a fence of pointed wooden stakes, and paling is a fence made of such pales.

clue.text: US indie company plans special version of Brains Trust …

indicators.note: a new version is a reworking, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
CO is the abbreviation for company
taken as written
S is an abbreviation for special

explanation.surface: An American independent film company is planning a special remake of an old programme.
explanation.walkthrough: The Brains Trust was a BBC radio and TV programme in which a panel of experts answered listeners' questions. The ellipsis carries on into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The Brains Trust format was a group of experts debating questions, which is an example of a panel discussion.

clue.text: … might he enjoy it once weekly?

definitions.text: … might he enjoy it once weekly?

parts.words: might he enjoy it once weekly?
parts.note: surface reading: a fan who tuned in every week to the programme in the previous clue; setter's reading: also points to a magazine of that name that the BBC published weekly until 1991

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links back to the Brains Trust, a radio show, so the person enjoying it is someone hearing it; 'once weekly' also nods to the BBC's former weekly magazine of the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who tunes in to a radio broadcast is one who hears it, the usual word for a member of a radio audience.

clue.text: Rod Peacock?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a bar or brace in a framework
second meaning: to peacock is to walk proudly showing off

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a person's name, Rod Peacock; 'Peacock' is a verb here, and the question mark flags that unusual sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A brace in a structure is a bar of that name, and a showy, swaggering walk like a peacock's is the verb.

clue.text: Lecturer visiting island tied up? Shocking!

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means everything is read from bottom to top

parts.note: Elba is the Mediterranean island of Napoleon's exile

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside someone's place, so the letter sits within the following word

parts.note: roped means tied up with rope
L is the abbreviation for lecturer

explanation.surface: A lecturer visiting an island is bound up, which is shocking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tied up' looks like one phrase, but 'up' belongs to the reversal and applies to the island and the tying together. Elba is where Napoleon was first exiled.
explanation.definitionFit: Something deplorable deserves strong condemnation, which is what shocking conduct is.

clue.text: No sailors either from Northumberland?

parts.note: 'no ... either' is expressed by nor, as in 'nor did they'
the sailors are 'the RN', the Royal Navy

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether there are any sailors from Northumberland, either.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not the Royal Navy either' can be put as NOR THE RN. Northumberland is England's northernmost county, so a person from there is northern.
explanation.definitionFit: Northumberland borders Scotland at the top of England, so anything from there is in the north.

clue.text: It's heavenly playing harp on the banks of the Seine

indicators.note: in an across entry, one piece put on another comes after it
a river's banks are its edges, so the first and last letters of the Seine are used
playing means the letters of harp are toyed with and rearranged

explanation.surface: Heavenly music from a harpist on the banks of the Seine in Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: SE, the 'banks of' the Seine, then RAPH, HARP rearranged ('playing').
explanation.definitionFit: A seraph is an angel of the highest order, a being that belongs to heaven.

clue.text: Cello and cornet I played for Remembrance

indicators.note: music that is played is performed afresh, so these letters are worked into a new order

parts.note: the two instruments and the I, taken as written; 'and' only joins them

explanation.surface: A cellist, a cornet player and the speaker perform at a Remembrance service.
explanation.walkthrough: Remembrance Sunday honours Britain's war dead, often with music, which makes the surface plausible; here the word is just the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Recollection is the act of recalling something to mind, a synonym of remembrance.

clue.text: Shining age with true possibilities for fliers

parts.note: lit means lighted, shining
an era is an age

indicators.note: the possibilities of true are the other arrangements of its letters

explanation.surface: A bright age of real opportunity for aviators.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fliers' looks like aviators, but it means flyers: printed leaflets. LIT, ERA, then the letters of TRUE in another order.
explanation.definitionFit: Literature can mean printed matter such as leaflets and brochures, which fliers are.

clue.text: Spike Milligan's last bow's enthralling

indicators.note: to enthral is to hold captive, so one piece holds the other within it

parts.note: a bow is a kind of tie; the 's is 'is'

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter, the only one kept

parts.note: the final letter of the surname

explanation.surface: Spike Milligan, the comedian, takes his final bow to an enthralled audience.
explanation.walkthrough: Spike Milligan was a British comic and Goon Show star, so 'Spike' looks like part of his name; it is the definition alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A tine is a sharp prong, as on a fork or antler, which is a kind of spike.

clue.text: Setter's a hoot, we hear — that's sweet

indicators.note: what we hear is a sound, so the answer is spelt differently from how the phrase is said

parts.note: the setter is 'I', and to be a hoot is to be a scream: 'I scream'

explanation.surface: The setter boasts of being hilarious, and rather sweet too.
explanation.walkthrough: In crosswords the setter refers to themselves as I or me. Both a hoot and a scream mean a very funny person.
explanation.definitionFit: Ice cream is a frozen dessert, and in Britain a dessert is often called a sweet.

clue.text: Pen erotic composition, do!

indicators.note: a composition is something put together, so these letters are assembled anew

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An exhortation to write a steamy piece of writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do' at the end looks like the verb urging you to write; it is the noun for a party.
explanation.definitionFit: A do is an informal word for a social gathering, and a reception is a formal party such as one after a wedding.

clue.text: VIP is present in heart of procession

parts.note: PR is an abbreviation for present, as in the present tense in grammar

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its central stretch, here the middle four letters of procession

explanation.surface: A dignitary attends, right at the centre of a parade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' is a link word. PR for present (the grammatical tense) is a rare abbreviation; CESS is the central four letters of procession.
explanation.definitionFit: A royal daughter counts as a very important person at any public event.

clue.text: Brilliant system of measurement captures extremes of El Niño

indicators.note: something captured is held inside, so the letters are placed within the word

parts.note: the metric system is a measuring system

indicators.note: the extremes are the two ends, so the first and last letters are taken

parts.note: the first and last letters of the phrase

explanation.surface: A weather scientist's measuring system captures the extreme effects of El Niño.
explanation.walkthrough: El Niño is a Pacific weather pattern, so 'extremes' suggests extreme weather; here it means only end letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A meteoric career is dazzlingly rapid and spectacular, like a meteor's bright streak, hence brilliant.

clue.text: Sect exposed in actuality oddly dissolving

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters melt away, leaving only the even ones

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: A religious sect is exposed, and in reality it is gradually breaking up.
explanation.definitionFit: A cult is a small religious group with unorthodox beliefs, often called a sect.

clue.text: Bromide, after initially tasting, is swallowed in liquor

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the first letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

indicators.note: something swallowed ends up inside, so it goes within the drink

parts.note: rum is a spirit, a liquor
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sedative, once tasted, is gulped down with a stiff drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Bromide was once given as a sedative, which suits the drink in the surface; here it means a dull, stale remark.
explanation.definitionFit: A bromide is a trite, unoriginal saying, and a truism is a statement so obvious it is hardly worth making.

clue.text: Where fighter comes in to disrobe on stairhead?

parts.note: the landing is the level space at the head of a flight of stairs
to strip is to undress

explanation.surface: A boxer enters the house and undresses at the top of the stairs.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces come in reverse of clue order: 'on stairhead' puts the stair word first. 'Fighter' suggests a boxer, but it is a fighter plane.
explanation.definitionFit: A fighter aircraft touches down on a runway, which in a makeshift airfield is called by this name.

clue.text: Implication of Penny's separation …

parts.note: D stood for the old British penny, from the Latin denarius; the 's is 'has'
a rift is a split or separation

explanation.surface: The meaning behind a woman called Penny's separation from her partner.
explanation.walkthrough: Penny looks like a woman's name; it is the coin. Before 1971, British pennies were written d.
explanation.definitionFit: The drift of what someone says is its general meaning or tenor, the point it implies.

clue.text: … was initially maturity of income

indicators.note: initially means at the beginning, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the word
to come of age is to reach maturity

explanation.surface: Continuing from the previous clue: the separation was at first a matter of mature income.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis joins this to the clue before to make one long surface, but the two clues are separate.
explanation.definitionFit: A wage is regular pay for work, so it is income.

clue.text: Otiose and deceitful — take a month off and regroup

indicators.note: to regroup is to rearrange into a new formation, so the remaining letters are reordered
taking something off removes it, here the short form of a calendar month

parts.note: taken as written
Dec is the abbreviation for December; these letters are removed

explanation.surface: A lazy and dishonest worker is told to take a month's leave and pull themselves together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Otiose' looks like a partner of 'deceitful' in a list of faults, but it is the whole definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Otiose means serving no practical purpose, which is the meaning of futile, pointless.

clue.text: Pernicious Cadillac I'm in is deficient in reverse

indicators.note: going backwards means the letters are read from right to left
deficient means lacking something, so the outer letters of the phrase are missing

parts.note: letters running across the words, with the ends of the phrase missing

explanation.surface: The Cadillac I'm sitting in is harmful because it is defective and stuck in reverse gear.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts inside Cadillac and ends at the start of 'is'; read backwards, it gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Inimical means harmful or hostile, close to pernicious, which means causing great harm.

clue.text: Get rid of reported mole on lad's side

indicators.note: a report is what is said, so the word is spelt by how it sounds

parts.note: a mole is a stone pier or breakwater, also called a jetty
a son is a lad; the 's belongs to the surface

explanation.surface: Getting rid of a mole that has been spotted on a boy's flank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mole' suggests a skin blemish or a burrowing animal; here it is a harbour wall. 'On lad's side' puts the boy piece next to it.
explanation.definitionFit: To jettison is to throw cargo overboard, so more generally to discard or get rid of.

clue.text: Crib graduate's new limitless source of ideas

parts.note: MA is a Master of Arts, a graduate
N is the abbreviation for new

indicators.note: without its limit means the word's end boundary is cut off, losing its last letter

parts.note: the germ of an idea is its origin; its last letter is dropped

explanation.surface: A student copies from a graduate's fresh and endless fund of ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crib' looks like a verb meaning copy; it is the noun for a feeding trough or a baby's cot.
explanation.definitionFit: A crib is a feeding rack for animals, and a manger is the trough or box from which livestock eat.
